{"id": "14:44/q17", "question": "What did 'you have no departure' deny?", "turns_on": "Whether zawāl means death, movement to resurrection, escape from punishment, change of faith or residence, or loss of worldly power.", "positions": [{"id": "14:44/q17/p1", "position": "They denied leaving this world or the grave for resurrection, reckoning and the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, Mujāhid and many others relate it to the oath in 16:38 that God would not raise the dead. Al-Rāzī rejects mere ordinary changes of age, wealth or death: the denial is transfer to recompense. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says it is departure from earth after death; Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies leaving graves for reckoning and says the complement is implicit. Asad notes the literal image of no going down or removal. Al-Suddī glosses resurrection after death. Kuranyolu adds denial of punishment. Nuances between world, earth, graves and recompense are stated by these sources."}, {"id": "14:44/q17/p2", "position": "They claimed they would never die or cease to live in this world.", "reasons": "Mujāhid reports Quraysh's oath that they would not die or pass away; al-Ṭabarī preserves another report from him. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī allow this permanence reading. Abū Ḥayyān objects that wrongdoers admitted death and explicitly rejects the reading he attributes to Mujāhid. Bursawī recalls an arrogant oath never to leave worldly life. Al-Ālūsī allows denial of departure from worldly enjoyment."}, {"id": "14:44/q17/p3", "position": "They thought they could not escape or leave punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan gives this interpretation, and al-Qurṭubī reports it as a second reading."}, {"id": "14:44/q17/p4", "position": "They asserted they would not leave disbelief for faith.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī includes this among three senses of resisting a changed status quo."}, {"id": "14:44/q17/p5", "position": "They asserted they would not leave their homes or settled lands.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī includes remaining at home. In the related account Kināna tells Kaʿb that his people will remain in their inherited gardens and vineyards, backed by enduring ancestors, armor and swords, and will make opponents yield."}, {"id": "14:44/q17/p6", "position": "They would not leave their present condition for the state they now request.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās gives this gloss, transmitted by al-Durr."}, {"id": "14:44/q17/p7", "position": "Their power and defenses made their community permanently dominant.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the implied speaker exposes their earlier confidence and asks why they now beg for time."}]}
{"id": "14:44/q18", "question": "How does 'mā lakum min zawāl' relate grammatically to the oath?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause supplies the oath's answer or is a separate divine response to the plea.", "positions": [{"id": "14:44/q18/p1", "position": "It is the answer or content of their oath, recast in second person for direct rebuke.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī calls it reported speech matching the grammatical form of 'you swore.' Al-Nasafī, al-Samīn and Ibn ʿĀshūr say a literal oath would use 'we,' while the rebuke keeps 'you.' Al-Ālūsī adds that min strengthens negation. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the second clause explains the oath without a separate implicit quotation."}, {"id": "14:44/q18/p2", "position": "It is God's answer to their current plea; the oath's answer is omitted.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this as a less apparent construction: 'what means have you to depart this state?' He favors the direct oath-answer reading."}]}
{"id": "14:44/q19", "question": "What report places this plea within the requests of Hell's inhabitants?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:44/q19/p1", "position": "The people of Hell ask to obey if delayed, and are rebuked by their oath and predecessors' dwellings.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī reports the scene and God's answer extending into 14:45–46. Al-Durr says the account reached him; Abū Ḥayyān places the address while they are in Hell."}, {"id": "14:44/q19/p2", "position": "This is one of five pleas; four receive answers and the fifth ends in silence.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ālūsī cite al-Bayhaqī's transmission from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb. The related pleas and replies cite 40:11–12, 32:12–14, this verse, 35:37, and, in al-Ālūsī's account, 23:106–108; afterward they gasp or groan without hope."}]}
{"id": "14:44/q20", "question": "What effect can verbal repetition and similar endings have?", "turns_on": "How strongly sound similarity sets up an expectation of repetition, and whether the repeated forms serve a useful meaning.", "positions": [{"id": "14:44/q20/p1", "position": "Useful meaning makes wordplay effective; mere strained repetition does not.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī criticizes Abū al-Fatḥ al-Bustī's strained examples and praises repetitions that serve an apt thought."}, {"id": "14:44/q20/p2", "position": "Repeated endings create expectation, then surprise when the word changes.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says the delayed realization brings a sense of gain; where words differ from their beginnings, as in al-Buḥturī's example, the effect remains but is weaker."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q01", "question": "Who spoke these words to the Prophet, and what occasion is reported?", "turns_on": "The sources differ in whether they identify named Quraysh men or explain the wording by what the idolaters heard him say; neither account excludes the other.", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q01/p1", "position": "Meccan or Quraysh unbelievers addressed Muhammad; a report specifies Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.", "reasons": "Muqatil names the four men; Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi, and Elmalili transmit that identification. Ibn Atiyya names the first two and others like them. Al-Qurtubi says the speakers then asked him to bring angels as proof."}, {"id": "15:6/q01/p2", "position": "A report says Makkan idolaters heard Muhammad say that God had sent the Reminder down to him, prompting this wording.", "reasons": "Study Quran transmits the report as an explanation of their phrasing; it does not identify individual speakers."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q02", "question": "What is the Reminder here, and why is it called dhikr?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q02/p1", "position": "It is the Qur'an, God's revealed message, named for recitation and remembrance.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi from Ibn Abbas, al-Nasafi, al-Dahhak through al-Durr, al-Alusi, Elmalili, and Study Quran explicitly identify it as the Qur'an; al-Damghani and Kur'an Yolu render it revelation. Elmalili says it recalls divine admonition; Ibn Ashur says it is recited and repeated, reminds of God and the Last Day, and preserves remembrance for later generations (21:10; 43:44). Ibn Ashur calls this a comprehensive Qur'anic name previously unknown to Arabs and distinguishes Qur'an as naming intended recitation; both name discourse received and recited, like poetry, sermons, stories, and fables. Kur'an Yolu lists remembering, memorizing, mentioning, and praising as lexical senses, warning/admonition/revelation, previous scriptures, and the Qur'an as wider Qur'anic uses (16:43; 21:7,105; 15:9), and cites Tirmidhi, Merits of the Qur'an, report 14, for dhikr as a Qur'anic name. Study Quran notes other scriptures are dhikr elsewhere (16:43; 21:2,7; 40:53) but cites 15:9; 7:2; 16:44; 20:3; 36:11 for this referent. Ibn Ashur also gives the basic senses verbal utterance and recollection."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q03", "question": "How is the descent clause read?", "turns_on": "The reports vary in verb form, voice, and whether the alternative 'cast down' wording is a reading or a gloss that differs from the mushaf text.", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q03/p1", "position": "The common reading has nuzzila, with a doubled consonant and passive voice.", "reasons": "Al-Samin labels it the reading of the generality."}, {"id": "15:6/q03/p2", "position": "Zayd ibn Ali reads nazala, light and active.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin report this form as Zayd's reading."}, {"id": "15:6/q03/p3", "position": "Zayd ibn Ali reads nazzala actively, with al-dhikr raised as its subject.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this form; its doubled consonant differs from the light active form reported by Abu Hayyan and al-Samin."}, {"id": "15:6/q03/p4", "position": "The wording 'the one to whom the Reminder was cast down' is reported as a reading or explanatory gloss.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya attributes it to al-A'mash; Abu Hayyan attributes it to Zayd ibn Ali and treats it as explanatory because its consonants differ from the written mushaf. Al-Alusi reports Abu Hayyan's preferred treatment as a gloss for the same reason; the transmitters named for the wording vary."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q04", "question": "Whose words are the address, and what does its apparent admission of revelation mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the entire quoted sentence belongs to the mockers, or God supplies the vocative while they utter only the charge.", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q04/p1", "position": "The whole address is the unbelievers' sarcastic speech: 'the one to whom the Reminder descended' means according to his or his followers' claim, not their belief.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas through al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi reasons that believers in the descent could not simultaneously call him mad. Abu Ali al-Farisi supplies the implicit 'according to you/your followers' and compares sarcastic titles at 44:49 and 43:49; al-Wahidi's reports from Zahra al-Yaman and Jarir illustrate repeating an epithet from its bearer's own self-assessment. Al-Farisi says Arabic can voice an alleged claim with this understood qualification. Ibn Atiyya compares calling an ignorant person a scholar unable to perform ablution. Al-Razi cites Pharaoh and Shuayb's people (26:27; 11:87), plus ironic good news (3:21); al-Nasafi cites the same parallel

s and calls the wording a deliberate reversal. Ibn Ashur says the vocative publicly spotlights the description, the relative clause makes claimed revelation the ground of mockery, and such a title follows its referent's claim rather than the speaker's belief. Ibn Kathir adds 'merely claims' revelation. Al-Alusi favors the related explanation that the extraordinary claim itself supplies their supposed evidence of madness."}, {"id": "15:6/q04/p2", "position": "Only 'you are mad' is the unbelievers' speech; God supplies the address to clear the Prophet of the accusation.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this from some interpreters but objects that it fits the next verse's rebuttal poorly, while allowing that the next verse could answer the unbelievers' implication."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q05", "question": "What does the passive wording of 'sent down' imply?", "turns_on": "Al-Alusi gives two possible targets for the passive's denial: the claimed descent's agent or its occurrence upon Muhammad.", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q05/p1", "position": "It distances the mockers from accepting revelation's divine source, as if the descent has no acknowledged agent.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai says their passive phrasing reflects denial of revelation itself; al-Alusi says it can suggest the claimed descent has no agent. Tabatabai says passive voice distances them from its alleged source, alongside the derisive title and charge."}, {"id": "15:6/q05/p2", "position": "It directs denial to the claim that the Reminder descended upon Muhammad, rather than to identifying its sender.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi explicitly offers this as another implication of the passive."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q06", "question": "Why is 'upon him' brought forward in the descent clause?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q06/p1", "position": "The order highlights their denial that a Reminder descends from God, whereas 43:31 challenges the chosen recipient after accepting the source of revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi contrasts this wording with 43:31 to distinguish the objections."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q07", "question": "What does majnun mean in this accusation?", "turns_on": "Whether majnun denotes ordinary madness or a connection to jinn in the opponents' usage.", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q07/p1", "position": "It is the ordinary accusation of madness; its root denotes covering or being covered.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi gives verb forms for becoming or being made mad and explains dense, intertwined plants called majnun because their parts cover one another. The many reports of their calling Muhammad mad use this ordinary sense."}, {"id": "15:6/q07/p2", "position": "In pagan usage it may mean a person connected with jinn, rather than simply an insane person.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports Ateş's proposed sense, alongside its account of pagan belief that jinn inspire poets."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q08", "question": "Was the charge of madness intended literally or as a taunt?", "turns_on": "Whether the opponents meant an actual diagnosis or used madness as figurative abuse.", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q08/p1", "position": "It could be a metaphorical or derisive charge.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports commentators who allow metaphorical mockery; other commentators describe the whole address and accusation as sarcastic or derisive."}, {"id": "15:6/q08/p2", "position": "They could have literally believed he was mad.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports this possibility from commentators; the faint-like state during revelation and the implausibility they perceived in his prophetic claim are given elsewhere as possible grounds."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q09", "question": "What made the opponents call Muhammad mad?", "turns_on": "The proposed grounds differ: the apparent impossibility of the message, Muhammad's state during revelation, or a belief that jinn inspired what they called poetry.", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q09/p1", "position": "They judged his claim of divine revelation and prophethood, and the teaching based on it, too implausible to be sane.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says they considered a true messenger from God impossible and his teaching beyond reason. Al-Baydawi says the claim of God's sending the Qur'an sounded like a madman's speech; al-Nasafi says the same. Ibn Kathir specifies his call to follow him and abandon inherited religion. Al-Biqai says they alleged a jinn confused him because he claimed God sent a Reminder. Al-Alusi prefers this explanation as best suited to the context, comparing someone deemed mad for an incredible assertion. Elmalili says they rejected his warnings and prophethood as irrational; Kur'an Yolu transmits al-Razi's version."}, {"id": "15:6/q09/p2", "position": "His faint-like or absorbed state during revelation was mistaken for madness or jinn possession.", "reasons": "Al-Razi mentions other verses denying the charge (68:51–52; 7:184). Al-Alusi reports this explanation. Elmalili says they cited his absorbed state as supposed evidence; Kur'an Yolu transmits al-Razi's near-trance and jinn-possession formulation."}, {"id": "15:6/q09/p3", "position": "They treated the Qur'an as poetry inspired by jinn rather than revelation from God.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu says pre-Islamic pagans thought poets received verse from jinn and applies that assumption to Muhammad's contemporaries, citing 21:5 and 37:36. Ateş's proposed sense of majnun as jinn-connected fits this conception."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q10", "question": "How does this saying develop the preceding passage?", "turns_on": "The links emphasize different earlier material: warnings and objections or the command in 15:3.", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q10/p1", "position": "It presents the unbelievers' objections after threats and warnings, with insult taking the place of an answer.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says God turns from emphasizing threats to their objections to Muhammad's claim. Al-Jishumi says they answer the warning with mockery. Al-Biqai says the accusation substitutes for an answer to the preceding argument and exposes stubbornness (15:4–5). Al-Alusi says the passage depicts the Meccans' rejection of the bearer and the Book and the outcome awaiting them."}, {"id": "15:6/q10/p2", "position": "It is conjoined to the command to leave them in 15:3, depicting deeper disbelief and denial beyond their indulgence and hopes.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reads 15:6 as continuing 15:3: leave them to disbelieve and utter every kind of denial and mockery."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q11", "question": "How does the next verse respond to this accusation?", "turns_on": "Whether the following verse is read chiefly as the opponents' further demand or as a rebuttal relevant to the proposed division of speech.", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q11/p1", "position": "After calling him mad, the opponents demand angels as evidence of his truthfulness.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi recounts their move from the insult in 15:6 to the angel demand in 15:7."}, {"id": "15:6/q11/p2", "position": "The next verse rebuts the unbelievers' implied claim even if God supplied the vocative in this verse.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi allows that 15:7 could answer the implication but says it fits poorly if only 'you are mad' is their speech."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q12", "question": "How is this taunt paralleled or answered elsewhere in the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "The cited verses serve different roles: earlier parallels to the taunt and direct denials of the charge.", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q12/p1", "position": "Pharaoh and other peoples similarly charged messengers with madness or used praise ironically.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, and al-Alusi compare Pharaoh's address to Moses (26:27). Al-Razi adds Shuayb's people's ironic praise (11:87) and ironic glad tidings of punishment (3:21); al-Nasafi cites those comparisons too. Elmalili invokes Pharaoh's accusation. Study Quran says possession was charged against Moses, Noah, and Muhammad and cites 23:70; 34:8; 44:14; 51:39,52; 68:51; 26:27; 54:9."}, {"id": "15:6/q12/p2", "position": "Other verses explicitly deny that Muhammad is mad.", "reasons": "Abu Ali al-Farisi points to the answer in 68:2, 'By your Lord's blessing, you are not mad.' Al-Razi cites 68:51–52 and 7:184 against the accusation."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q13", "question": "What broader pattern or purpose does this mockery illustrate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q13/p1", "position": "The opponents repeat the mockery of earlier messengers and face their predecessors' fate; the sura consoles Muhammad while warning and offering hope.", "reasons": "Islahi states the repeated pattern and shared fate. Tabatabai says the sura addresses their mockery, dismissal of the Qur'an as mad rambling, and counsels patience and forbearance with warning and glad tidings. Ibn Ashur says they are to be left to their denial and mockery; al-Alusi frames the passage as rejection of both the messenger and Book with a coming outcome."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q14", "question": "What report illustrates how the Prophet answered the polytheists' abuse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q14/p1", "position": "He told Aisha that God diverted their abuse because they insulted 'Mudhammam' while he was Muhammad.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports the Prophet's statement to Aisha as an example of the abuse directed at him."}]}
{"id": "15:6/q15", "question": "What happened when al-Hubab asked whether the Prophet's Badr position was revealed or tactical?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:6/q15/p1", "position": "The Prophet said it was strategy; al-Hubab advised securing the nearest water, blocking wells behind it, and filling a basin, and the Prophet approved and acted on the advice.", "reasons": "Ibn Hisham transmits al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir's exchange; the report distinguishes a divinely fixed position from tactical judgment."}]}

"It is a majestic plural and repeated emphasis asserting that God Himself reveals and preserves the Reminder.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas identifies the plural with God alone; language scholars, al-Razi, and older scholars compare royal usage. Al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Baydawi, Biqai, Bursevi, Alusi, Ibn Ashur, Tabatabai, and Islahi connect the emphases to refuting mockery, excluding human or jinn authorship, and magnifying God and revelation; Ibn Ashur likens 63:1's use of an opponent's premise."}]}
{"id": "15:9/q02", "question": "What is the grammatical role of naḥnu?", "turns_on": "Whether naḥnu is parsed as a subject, emphasis of inna's noun, or a separating pronoun.", "positions": [{"id": "15:9/q02/p1", "position": "It is a subject whose predicate is nazzalnā, and that clause is the predicate of inna.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi gives the complete analysis. Al-Kawashi, al-Samin and al-Alusi accept subjecthood. Ibn Ashur calls the pronoun separating in the rhetorical analysis, while the others deny a technical separator because of the following clause or absence of two nouns."}, {"id": "15:9/q02/p2", "position": "It is an emphatic pronoun for the noun of inna.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi calls it accusative emphasis; al-Samin and al-Alusi also allow emphatic status, rejecting separation as the technical parse."}, {"id": "15:9/q02/p3", "position": "It serves as a separating pronoun that sharpens the affirmation.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur uses this rhetorical description and compares 63:1; al-Qurtubi, al-Samin, al-Kawashi and al-Alusi explicitly dispute a technical separator analysis because the next expression is a clause rather than the required second noun."}]}
{"id": "15:9/q03", "question": "What does nazzalnā convey about revelation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:9/q03/p1", "position": "God Himself sent the Qur'an down gradually, through Gabriel to Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf and Biqai specify Gabriel; Biqai excludes humans and jinn as authors. Tabatabai excludes Muhammad and angels as independent sources. Asad cites Zamakhshari on the verbal form and 2:23 for gradual revelation; Asad's translation says 'in stages'."}]}
{"id": "15:9/q04", "question": "What does al-dhikr denote here?", "turns_on": "Whether dhikr identifies the Qur'an as a text, highlights its admonition, or also conveys honor.", "positions": [{"id": "15:9/q04/p1", "position": "The Reminder is the Qur'an revealed to Muhammad.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Mawardi's Hasan and Dahhak, Wahidi's general exegetes, Damghani, Qurtubi, Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi, Alusi, Asad, Kuranyolu and Study Quran identify it. Kuranyolu ties it to the Book of 15:1; Study Quran to 15:6. Damghani cites 21:50 and 43:5, Elmalili cites 21:24 and 3:58 and notes the Qur'an's other names al-Hukm and ruh (42:52). Tabatabai argues the definite article points back to the previously mentioned Reminder, and rejects extending the promise to Torah and Gospel merely because they too are called remembrance."}, {"id": "15:9/q04/p2", "position": "The word evokes admonition and the revealed reminder of duties and rulings.", "reasons": "Jishumi allows a reminder of obligations and rulings. Biqai reads admonition together with honor. Tabatabai says the Qur'an recalls God's names, acts, angels, messengers, law, resurrection and final destinies, and that all its teachings recall Him."}, {"id": "15:9/q04/p3", "position": "The word also signifies honor for those who hold to the Book.", "reasons": "Jishumi cites 43:44; Biqai combines honor with admonition; al-Kashifi, quoted by Bursevi, says the Book brings worldly and otherworldly honor, citing 23:71."}]}
{"id": "15:9/q05", "question": "What does al-dhikr do for its recipients?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:9/q05/p1", "position": "It heals, clarifies, guides and guards those destined for felicity from disobedience.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata names healing, mercy, clarification and criterion. Sulami also transmits Ja'far's statement that God's preservation accompanies those for whom He wills good throughout life. Al-Mawardi says God keeps the Qur'an in hearts He wills good for, and removes it from hearts of those He wills evil for."}]}
{"id": "15:9/q06", "question": "To whom does lahu refer?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding explicit noun or the implicitly understood recipient of revelation supplies the antecedent.", "positions": [{"id": "15:9/q06/p1", "position": "It refers to Muhammad: God protects him from harm, enemies and plots.", "reasons": "Al-Farra and other transmitters use this reading; Baghawi, Zamakhshari, Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and Alusi support it with 5:67. Ibn al-Anbari, as reported by Razi, says the recipient is understood from revelation, comparing 97:1; Wahidi's report of him instead favors the Qur'an. Elmalili adds jinn and Satan; Kuranyolu cites the Prophet's survival and successful spread of Islam and says this also indirectly preserves revelation. Qurtubi also reports a narrower protection from falsely claiming something about God or having such a claim made against him."}, {"id": "15:9/q06/p2", "position": "It refers to the Reminder, the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Tabari and most later commentators take the nearest stated antecedent. Ibn al-Anbari as reported by Wahidi prefers it because revelation and revealed object already imply the recipient, comparing the unexpressed Qur'an in 97:1; Wahidi and Razi call it the apparent sense. Razi cites 41:42 and 4:82; Ibn Kathir invokes context; Tabatabai rejects the Prophet antecedent because 15:6's mockery turns on the Qur'an. Ibn Ashur calls the preservation clause parenthetic. Elmalili calls the Prophet reading sound but less apparent; Kuranyolu says both protections can be combined."}]}
{"id": "15:9/q07", "question": "How do the grammar and order of the preservation clause work?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "15:9/q07/p1", "position": "The nominal clause and active participle present an emphatic, continuing or future guarantee; the fronted object and lām strengthen it.", "reasons": "Alusi reports commentators who hear continuous miraculous protection. Tabatabai says the active participle normally points forward; Ibn Ashur says the lām reinforces the verb's force after its object and calls the waw parenthetic. Alusi says the paired clauses magnify God and revelation."}]}
{"id": "15:9/q08", "question": "What does God's preservation of the Reminder encompass?", "turns_on": "Whether the promise addresses textual integrity, heavenly keeping, continuing law, or retention in chosen people.", "positions": [{"id": "15:9/q08/p1", "position": "The Qur'an is kept intact against addition, omission, distortion, replacement and loss over time.", "reasons": "Qatada and Thabit specify Satan's inability to insert falsehood or remove truth; Tabari, Zajjaj, Baghawi, Qatada, Razi, Study Quran and Tabatabai invoke 41:42, while Razi and Study Quran also cite 4:82. Muqatil counters the charge of satanic teaching; Bursevi and Alusi include attacks, denial and mockery as ineffectual. Ibn Ashur includes non-vanishing and mass transmission from the Prophet's lifetime. Tabatabai limits the inference to changes that erase the text's character as remembrance: a repeated verse, dot or inflection with no such effect remains logically possible. Asad says early diacritic and vocalization variants usually change no meaning and mentions 85:22. Kuranyolu distinguishes protection during revelation from later preservation until Resurrection; Tabatabai includes order only where altered order destroys remembrance."}, {"id": "15:9/q08/p2", "position": "God keeps the Reminder with Himself.", "reasons": "Mujahid's gloss is 'with Us'; Tabari and al-Durr transmit it."}, {"id": "15:9/q08/p3", "position": "Preservation includes its presence in the hearts and lives of those God chooses.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata says God preserves it in His friends' hearts and employs the elect's limbs in its service; al-Mawardi links retention and removal to God's will for good or evil; Ibn Atiyya reports storing it in people's breasts."}, {"id": "15:9/q08/p4", "position": "God keeps it until it is requited for at Judgment Day, or keeps its revealed law in force until Resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi reports al-Hasan's requital reading; Alusi reports al-Hasan's understanding of continuing law.
